cards.front: The shape of a nearby-places system
cards.back: Places change rarely and searches are constant, so build a read-optimized spatial index next to the search servers with a normal database behind it.

cards.front: Size of the geo index for 500M places
cards.back: 24 bytes each (id, lat, lng) is 12 GB, perhaps 20-30 GB with tree overhead. Every search server can hold a full copy in RAM.

cards.front: Why clients round their location to about 50 m
cards.back: Nearby users' queries become identical and cacheable for a few seconds.

cards.front: Why plain SQL lat/lng ranges are slow
cards.back: A B-tree index helps one column only, so the database scans a huge strip of the world for the other.
One cell size fits nowhere: cells in Manhattan hold thousands of places and cells in the ocean hold none.

cards.front: How a quadtree adapts to density
cards.back: Start with one cell; split any cell with more than about 500 places into four. About 10 levels for 500M places.

cards.front: Geohash cell sizes at lengths 5, 6 and 7

cards.back: So 5 stars from 3 reviews doesn't beat 4.6 from 800.

cards.front: How 'open now' avoids a database call
cards.back: An opening-hours bitmap is kept alongside the ids in memory with category and price.

cards.front: Full replicas vs sharding the index
cards.back: At 12-30 GB every server holds the whole index. Once it outgrows memory, hash by place id and merge each shard's top-k in an aggregator.
Change data capture from the places database onto Kafka; servers apply deltas, and a nightly snapshot lets new servers load in minutes.

cards.front: Where reviews and rating averages live
cards.back: Reviews in a wide-column store partitioned by place; averages maintained incrementally in Redis, never computed from raw reviews on search.

quiz.q: Searches in Manhattan scan thousands of candidates while rural searches find nothing nearby. The index is a fixed 10-mile grid. What fixes both?
choices: A quadtree that splits dense cells and keeps sparse cells large
quiz.why: Quadtree cells are small where places are dense and large where they are sparse.

quiz.q: Thousands of users a minute search 'restaurants near Times Square' and the index is overloaded at lunch. What takes most load off?
choices: Round locations and cache results per cell and filters for 30-60 s
quiz.why: Identical queries in popular areas can be cached briefly.

quiz.q: The index is sharded by place id and p99 latency is set by one slow shard. What helps?
choices: Send a hedged request to a replica when one shard is slow
quiz.why: Scatter-gather tail latency depends on the slowest shard; hedging cuts it.

quiz.q: A newly added café doesn't appear in search after an hour. Which signal points to the cause?
choices: Index lag between the newest applied change and now
quiz.why: Edits flow through CDC and Kafka; lag means servers aren't applying deltas.

quiz.q: A search server restarts. How does it get its index back quickly?
choices: Rebuild from a full database scan
Load the nightly snapshot, then replay the Kafka log since
Copy from a neighbour over HTTP
Start empty and fill from queries
quiz.why: Snapshot plus log replay loads the index in minutes.

quiz.q: A new place with three 5-star reviews tops results above a beloved spot rated 4.6 from 800 reviews. What should change?
choices: Smooth ratings so small review counts carry less weight
quiz.why: Smoothed ratings stop tiny samples from dominating.

quiz.q: A business posts a burst of glowing reviews from new accounts. How should the system respond?
choices: Score reviews with signals like account age and bursts, and hide suspicious ones from the rating
Show the reviews but sort them last
quiz.why: Trust scores keep fake reviews out of averages.
